newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Another S.Korean business group tapped for bailout.
newsitem.headline: Another S.Korean business group tapped for bailout.

text.p: One of South Korea's leading retailing and textile business groups was pulled from the brink of bankruptcy on Monday when its major creditor bank announced a rescue.

SEOULBANK said in a statement it would bail out Midopa Department Store, one of the country's oldest retailers, and Dainong Corp, a leading maker of textiles and apparel. Both are listed Dainong Group affiliates.
The bank said it would also bail out two unlisted Dainong affiliates, Dainong Heavy Industries Inc and Metro Product Co.
The four units accounted for 83 percent of the group's assets and 86 percent of its debts at the end of 1996, a SEOULBANK report said.
The failure of Midopa, an anchor of Seoul's fashionable Myongdong district, would have been a heavy blow to the country's business community, still reeling from string of corporate bankruptcies.
While the Dainong Group is not among the country's 30 chaebols or business conglomerates, it is an established, well-known group with 21 affiliates.
A SEOULBANK executive told reporters the bailout was part of an earlier agreement among South Korean banks to keep afloat promising companies staggering under heavy debts.
"We have decided to bail out the four companies in view of the impact their failure would have on society and the economy," bank executive director Lee Dong-man said.
The Dainong Group has been struggling under 1.84 trillion won ($2.1 billion) in debts as of the end of 1996, compared to total assets of 1.79 trillion won, a SEOULBANK report said.
The bailout decision would be formally approved at a May 28 meeting of 23 creditor banks, including SEOULBANK, Commercial Bank of Korea, Korea Long-Term Credit Bank and Hanil Bank, he said.
Lee said it was feared failure of the Dainong affiliates would cause huge job losses, exacerbate financial institutions' bad debts and send subcontractors into bankruptcy.
"Failures of Midopa and Dainong Corp would lead to the loss of about 6,500 jobs and cause the insolvency of about 4,600 subcontractors and related companies," Lee said.
A Dainong Group official said the group had been trying to sell off assets as well as some affiliates.
"We have been in the middle of restructuring work, but our restructuring plan was hit by a sudden takeover bid for Midopa," said the official, who declined to be identified.
He was referring to the hostile takeover bid in March by Shindongbang Corp. That bid fizzled out after another large shareholder of Midopa turned against Shindongbang.
The official said the group had been forced to concentrate resources on defending against the takeover.
Under the banks' bailout agreement, the credit lines of companies designated for rescue would remain open even after they defaulted on debt payments.

The first beneficiary of the agreement was the Jinro Group, the country's 19th largest conglomerate, which has been troubled by some 3.2 trillion won of debt. Six of Jinro's 24 affiliates have been designated for bailout and the group has put on sale some of its property and affiliates to raise cash.
South Korea has been rocked by the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March, both under heavy debts incurred mainly by excessive expansion.
Also hurting, the Ssangyong and Doosan business groups recently announced plans to sell assets and affiliates.
(Conversion: $1 = 892 won)
